title: Sasha Rush on Building Cursor Composer and the Future of Agentic Coding

segments.text: What was the vision behind composer?
>> At cursor, we had a previous model,
cursor tab, which was our autocomplete
model and it's one of the most popular
features in cursor. I think developers
really like it because it's really
snappy. It's kind of a delight to use
and you can kind of get your vision done
quickly. So, we wanted to build an agent
model that had similar properties. We
wanted it to be really smart and good at
coding, but also really fast so that it
would give you an answer quickly that
you could iterate on and kind of provide
more feedback as you went.
>> That was my first impression. I was
playing around with cursor 2.0 and the
first thing I said literally was it's
blazing fast. Was that like an
intentional decision?
>> Yeah, it was something that we found
really changed the experience that if
the model was fast enough, you could
really kind of keep in the flow of
coding. Um, that being said, there were
other fast models that we had seen
released before and we felt like they
weren't kind of at a sufficient coding
quality that we felt kind of comfortable
trusting them. So, we wanted a model
that we thought was smart enough that we
could trust to write code for ourselves,
uh, but also fast enough that it felt
really snappy
>> cuz I know I was reading in the
announcement like some of the
architecture decisions, right? Mixture
of experts and and reinforcement
learning. What was the thought process
as far as as the decisions there? Yeah.
So, um I think we've seen a lot of
models that really focus on having just
general ability that they're good at
writing essays or they're good at kind
of giving you dating advice. And we
really thought we could build a model
that was just very specialized for doing
one thing, which was being kind of an
agent model for coding. And
reinforcement learning is kind of the
tool that allows you to do that where uh
you kind of uh don't need to just train
on the web but can focus on a specific
sub area and build a kind of specialized
model that kind of just kills it at that
one task.
>> This is an agentic experience, right? So
it's different than like a simple LLM,
right, with reinforcement learning. So
how is that different as far as uh
building it?
>> Yeah. So, I didn't really get a sense
until I started kind of working on
coding models how crazy some of these uh
agent systems are in terms of how
powerful they can be in their tool call
use. We see models that casually call
150 tools to try to answer your
question. Uh and so we think kind of as
these models get better and better in
different areas, they're going to be
kind of both smart in what they do, but
also very smart in how they find
information. So if you have a very large
codebase, they're going to be calling
tools to do search. They're going to be
calling tools to run terminal commands.
And they can do a lot of stuff that
maybe a human would get bored of or kind
of stop doing to try to find their
answer. So for us, the agent power of
the model is really just the kind of
persistence in trying to find the answer
that you're looking for.
>> I know that you you're built with
PyTorch and Ray. What libraries have you
used or work or not work?
So particularly for the agent part of
the system what we found was critical is
that this model basically has to run a
full version of cursor as part of
training. So we basically uh were able
to encapsulate all of cursor in a kind
of virtual machine and then launch
hundreds of thousands of these virtual
machines so that we could do training.
And it has to basically be like cursor
because we wanted to simulate what a
real user experience would look like.
And so getting the infrastructure to
really make that work required kind of
scaling that up, making sure it could be
stateful, making sure it was robust. Uh
and that's a kind of specific challenge
to RL that we don't see in other sorts
of training.
>> Yeah, there's a big distributed uh
computing aspect probably there. What
other parts like which libraries was it
ray data? What
>> what was what worked? What did it kind
of that in that sense?
>> So we use ray all across our spectrum.
Nice. So uh I think there are five
places we found that we're like
explicitly using Ray in this whole
process. The the main one is that Ray
has become a kind of standard way of
doing the RL controller. So basically
writing the code that uh controls the RL
rollouts that you'd use. And Ray is a
nice choice there because when you're
doing code rollouts, you could do say a
hundred of them and they're all going to
take a different amount of time to
finish. That's because some of them
might get to the answer quickly or
others might run terminal calls or
things of that. And kind of controlling
that whole process with Ray was nice. We
also use Ray data for a lot of our data
processing. So there's all sorts of kind
of uh different data processing that
goes into the RL pipeline. One of the
systems that we built internally was
using array data to analyze the results.
We have all these rollouts at scale. We
want to see which ones are winning,
which ones are losing, what looks good
or what looks bad. and we can very
easily spin up array data job to go over
all of our rollouts, call LM to analyze
the different results and try to
understand what's working or what's not
in that setting.

>> also regarding mixture of experts for

of experts. How would you explain it to

>> Yeah, so um before I worked at Curser, I
was a professor and uh I would teach
classes on transformers and language
models. And we're in about year 8 of
transformers being like the dominant
architecture in almost everything in AI
and really not too much has changed from
the kind of core transformer
architecture. The one exception of this
was mixture of experts. So mixture of
experts is a kind of architectural
change to a core transformer where
instead of having a standard neural
network in one of the layers, you
instead have a a set of distributed
neural networks. And uh every time
through the model instead of uh touching
every parameter, you instead choose a
subset of them that you use. And there's
several benefits to this. One is that
you don't end up kind of paying the
computational cost for all of them. But
more importantly, it allows you to
distribute your computation. So when
training these models on many GPUs, we
can basically uh shard the experts onto
different um GPUs and and use only the
ones that are necessary for that that
run. And so that's kind of an instance
of where the kind of uh machine learning
and the systems parts have kind of
gotten together to try to kind of find
the the most efficient uh architecture.
